label: paragraph_title
text: NO PEACE YET:

label: text
text: Labour And The Negotiations.

label: text
text: No development giving promise of bringing the strike to an end has occurred since the stoppage began

label: text
text: on Tuesday morning. The General Council of Trades Union Congress is in constant session and the Executive of the Miners' Federation met for a time this morning after which several members proceeded to consult with the General Council and others went to the House of Commons.

label: text
text: In to-day's issue of the strike newspaper, the "British Worker," which is published by the General Council, a reply is made to the statement of the Prime Minister that the Government was prepared to resume negotiations immediately the general strike is called off. The reply states that at this stage, with no knowledge of the subsequent line of policy that the Government intends to pursue, the General Council cannot comply with the Prime Minister's request for the unconditional withdrawal of strike notices. It indicates its readiness to resume the negotiations for an honourable settlement, but adds that any preliminary parleys with a view to discovering a basis for negotiations can only be undertaken in a free and unfettered atmosphere.

label: text
text: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, the Labour Leader, has made the statement: "I am not letting a moment pass unused for some attempt to devise ways of peace and accommodation."

label: paragraph_title
text: OFFICIAL REVIEW.

label: paragraph_title
text: No Shortage of Food

label: text
text:
An official communique says:
No shortage of food is reported anywhere. There has been obstruction of food supplies at many places in the country, in some cases accompanied by violence. The Government, however, is dealing with it effectually.

label: text
text: In order to give widespread protection to those engaged in maintaining food supplies and other essential services in the London area, it is proposed to raise the number of special constables as quickly as possible.

label: text
text: Twenty-five thousand volunteers enrolled in London and the Home Counties yesterday, bringing the total in that area up to 75,000.

label: paragraph_title
text: OFFICER FINED.

label: text
text: The mining areas are quiet, the miners observing a peaceful attitude.

label: paragraph_title
text: Fish Supplies

label: text
text: With regard to fish supplies 182 vessels in all have landed to-day at various ports and their total catches will not be less than 2,000 tons. Emergency transport has been organised almost entirely, by the fishing industry itself, and is working efficiently.

label: text
text: The postal services, which at first suffered some delay, have improved to such extent that the London Post Offices were reported at five o'clock this afternoon to be practically clear.

label: text
text: Owing to lack of steamer transport, a considerable consignment of mails from various parts of England was conveyed to Belfast to-day by a destroyer from Liverpool.

label: text
text: Resumption of publication of newspapers is announced from all parts of the country. London journals which will re-appear to-morrow morning are the "Daily Telegraph," "Daily Express" and "Daily Mirror."

label: paragraph_title
text: The Stock Exchange.

label: text
text: On the Stock Exchange, while there is still little disposition to transact business, there is a feeling of confidence and securities display a very steady appearance, prices being well maintained.

label: text
text: The Great Western Railway states that additional trains on its system are being run in all parts of the country. The situation and prospects are bright and hourly improving. One of the best features is the steady maintenance of milk supplies.

text: "DID NOT REMEMBER."

label: text
text: European Throws Turbian Into

label: text
text: Mr. M. P. Concannon, who is a 2nd Lieutenant in the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps, was fined at the Magistracy this morning on charges of being drunk and disorderly and assaulting a police officer, following a brawl at Blake Pier in the small hours of this morning.

label: text
text: The case was heard by Mr. R. E. Lindsell, chief magistrate. Inspector Spear of Central Station had charge of the prosecution and Mr. Concannon was not legally represented.

label: text
text: Indian constable B474 said that he was on duty at Blake Pier, about 8.10 a.m., when defendant threw his turban into the harbour. On witness protesting, defendant struck him in the chest. He blew his whistle and several other Indian policemen went to his assistance. Defendant struggled and was taken into custody by a European sergeant. No A146.

label: paragraph_title
text: Friend Intervenes

label: text
text: Questioned by Inspector Spear, witness added that a European who was with defendant, tried to restrain him (defendant).

label: text
text: In response to a whistle call, Lance-Sergeant A. W. Banks (A146) went to Blake Pier. Defendant, said the sergeant, was in an officer's mess suit, and struggling with several Indian police constables. Defendant was the worse for drink but went quietly to the station on being asked to do so.

label: text
text: Answering Inspector Spear, Sergeant Banks said that force had to be used both to search defendant (who disliked being searched) and to get him to a cell.

label: text
text: His Worship remarked that it was clear from the evidence that defendant "started the row" by throwing the constable's turban into the water.

label: text
text: (Sergeant Banks also stated in the witness-box that the turban had evidently been recovered as it was lying on the Pier, fully unrolled, and wet, but he had not seen the recovery).

label: text
text: When asked to plead at the opening of the case, Mr. Concannon made a statement. On His Worship asking if he had anything further to state, Mr. Concannon said that he wished to repeat that according to his habit he would never dream of attacking an Indian policeman and must therefore have been under great provocation.

label: text
text: Mr. Concannon had previously admitted that he was under the influence of liquor, adding that he did not remember anything about the turban. He repeated his statement as to not recollecting the incident. He did not know how it had happened, and expressed his regret at having been involved.

label: text
text: Asked if he wished to call the friend who was with him at the time, Mr. Concannon said "No." His-Worship imposed a fine of

label: text
text: His Worship imposed a fine of $10 on the charge of being drunk and disorderly, and $25 for assaulting the police.

label: paragraph_title
text: TRUE ROMANCE.

label: text
text: SEEKING RELATIVES ROUND THE WORLD.

label: text
text: WAR "ECHO" HERE.

label: text
text:
To be seen Home by the Police to day is an American negro who is wandering round the world in search of relatives who became rich in the Spanish-American War, at the beginning of this century.
Moses Little is the man on this long search. Fairly well built except for lines in the face which betray a not too steadfast upbringing, he is under middle age. He has not been in Hongkong long but he has spent the better part of several hundred dollars (gold) during his stay. Still, he has enough money to see him back to the United States, it having been decided that he is not to stay.

label: text
text: On April 28, he presented himself at the Police Passport office for permission to go on to Manila. His action was auspicious and he was searched. On him was found a revolver, in a very smart holster, and 122 rounds of ammunition.

label: text
text: As far as Little knows, his people emigrated at the time of the Spanish-American War and have since made their pile. He once heard of them in England and later on believed them to be either in Singapore or Hongkong.

label: text
text: A remand was given by the Magistrate so that inquiries could be made.

label: text
text: This morning, Major C. Wilson imposed a nominal fine of $25 for possession of arms without permission, cautioned the man for not having a passport, ordered the confiscation of the weapon &c., and made the order for him to be sent away by the Police.

label: text
text: A farewell social to their Scout Master (Mr. C. H. Butcher) was given by the 4th Hongkong (Murray) Troops of the Boy Scouts on Thursday night, Mrs. Stopford and Mrs. Stone having charge of the arrangements for tea. Mr. Beldon, a past master of the troop, attended and in the course of the evening spoke with appreciation of the work of Mr. Butcher and of the need for supporting the officers by the Scout body. Mr. Butcher was then presented with an engraved cigarette case by Mrs. Stopford on behalf of the troop and suitably replied, Several songs and dances were given, Mr. Charles Olive being amongst those who entertained the audience.

label: text
text: HAS HE VANISHED?

label: text
text: Entrusted with $4,000 to pay into his firm's account, a shop coolie has been "posted missing" since yesterday afternoon, and the money has not reached its destination.

label: text
text: The accountant of a Chinese firm at No. 105, Queen's Road Central says that he handed the money over at 1:30 p.m. Instructions were given to the foki to pay it to the Wui Loong Bank, also of Queen's Road Central. As he did not return by 3 p.m., inquiries were made, and the police were communicated with. The cash had not been paid in.

label: text
text: THIEF ENTERS BY AN OPEN WINDOW.

label: text
text: JEWELLERY STOLEN.

label: text
text: Through a window which had been left open at night, a thief entered No. 8, Castle Road, the residence of Mr. C. H. W. Kew, managing director of Messrs. Rudolf Wolff and Kew, and stole jewellery and money to the value of $231.50.

label: text
text: The window led to a bedroom in the house. Mr. Kew is of the opinion that the burglar must have got in some time between midnight and 6 a.m. yesterday. A report has been made to the Police.
